title: The Good Cabinet
blurb: Ila sneaks into Field Allocation for proof, and finds the file that was written about her before she ever picked up a fid.

blocks.text: Behind me, Mags breathes again. Then she reaches over my shoulder and lays her palm flat on her own name, the way she does when a point is final, as if she could hold the pencil down.
"No site," I say. "No date. Nobody's signed as keeper."
"Then he hasn't finished choosing," says Mags. "Or he's written the rest of it down somewhere else."
I know exactly where somewhere else is.
At eight minutes to five I am standing in the rain in the yard behind the Bureau, with no pass, a bob in my pocket and a pencil behind my ear, waiting for a courier.

Mags has gone to her branch meeting. She said, "Don't do anything Management could sack you for," and I said I was already suspended, and she looked at me for a long moment and said, "That's not the same thing, love, and you know it." Then she buttoned the black book inside her donkey jacket and went.

Field Allocation's yard door opens for one reason after half past four. Same-Day brings the evening post up from the docks. The courier has a key, and he wedges the door with his foot while he carries the sacks in, and the night porter stands at the gatehouse and watches him in and out. For four years I watched it from the Registry window.

The day porter locks the gatehouse at a quarter to five. The night porter comes in on the number 9 tram. Today the 9 is stuck at the end of the lane behind a brewery lorry that is trying to reverse into a gap a size too small for it, and I can see the night porter through the tram's front window, standing at the doors with his flask, looking at his watch.
At four fifty-two exactly, a courier bicycle comes round the lorry, through the gate, and stops at my feet.
"Four fifty-two," says Ferdie. Then he sees who I am. "Ila. You're not supposed to be in here."
"I'm not in here," I say. "I'm in the yard."

He looks at the tram. He looks at the night porter, who is knocking on the driver's glass now. Ferdie's mouth goes flat. He knows whose fault it is that the man is late, and so do I. Every one of Ferdie's arrivals makes somebody near him late. This time the somebody is the only person who would have stopped me, and I came here at eight minutes to five because I knew it would be.
I don't like how that feels. I'm doing it anyway.
Ferdie unlocks the door, wedges it with his foot, swings the post sack off his back and carries it in to the shelf by the stairs. I walk in behind him.
"Two minutes," he says, not looking at me. "I don't do longer."
"I know you don't."
"Four fifty-four. You're welcome." He goes. The door swings shut behind him and the lock catches, and I am standing in the dark at the bottom of the Allocation stair, trespassing.
Above me, on the landing, a light comes on.
My heart goes so hard I can feel it in my ears. Someone in a purple tabard is coming down with a mop bucket, one step at a time, with a little radio clipped to her belt playing the football.
"Hello!" I say. "You in the purple. Could you watch that stair for me? Just for a minute?"
She stops on the bottom step and looks me up and down: work coat, wet hair, a pencil behind my ear. "Watch it do what, love?"
"Watch for anyone coming down. Anyone at all. I'll be in there." I point at Allocation's door. "One minute."
She laughs, a proper laugh, and puts her bucket down. "Go on, then. I've done that floor. I'm only doing the stairs."
"What's your name?"
"Bev."
"Thank you, Bev. I'm Ila."
"Course you are," says Bev, and props herself on her mop.

Allocation's door isn't locked. Nobody locks it, because nobody but Allocation could want what's in it. The office is long and low, desks in rows, the rain loud on the skylights, and down the window wall stand the grey cabinets where Allocation files the jobs Registry sends up. I know their order. I filed the other half of every one of those jobs, downstairs, for four years.
The Lantry Steps job is in the third drawer down, under its number, which I know by heart, because it was mine.
Inside is the complaint, anonymous, which I've seen before. Behind it is the routing slip, which I haven't.

Routing slips are dull. They say which section, which grade, which day. This one says Field Allocation, countersigned with initials I know from the bottom of a hundred memos: G.V. And in the box for the knotter, where it ought to say any Registry Clerk on emergency warrant, it says:
Clerk I. Brandt. Noon only. Reach 2.
My name. Typed. Before anybody had asked me anything.

On the day I was suspended, Gervase Vosper walked me down the front steps and told me Allocation had nobody spare that week and Registry had me. A favour to both of us. But Registry didn't have me. Allocation asked for me, by name and by reach, and for noon, because noon is when Cuthbert sat on the steps with his sandwich.
Somebody wanted a clerk who could untie two and no more. I'm the clerk.
I take a photograph of the slip with my phone. My hands are steady, which surprises me. I copy the wording into my notebook as well, in pencil, because phones get lost and pencil doesn't.
Then I go to the cabinet at the end of the row, the one with his name on it.

Every senior knotter in Allocation keeps a drawer: carbon copies of the dockets he certified, each pinned to the site sheet a junior filled in before the untie. A re-swing of the site on the morning of the job, so the knotter knows what he's walking into. Juniors fill them in, seniors initial them, the sheets go in the drawer, and nobody looks at them again. Standards never asks for them. Why would it? Standards swings the keeper after the fall and compares what fell with the count on the docket. If they match, the job is clean.
The first job in Vosper's drawer is a crane at Kettle Wharf. The site sheet, in a junior's round hand, says seven strands. Vosper's certified docket, in his slanting one, says five.
The second is the fountain at the old market. Sheet: six. Docket: four.
A rotten awning on Bridge Street. Sheet: five. Docket: three.

I go through the whole drawer, and I'm not long at it before I stop needing to. Every docket is two lower than its sheet. Not one lower, not three. Two. Back and back, to before I ever came to the Bureau.
The keeper on every job is a Porter. Every Porter took exactly what the docket said, because Standards swung each of them, and their falls matched, and there's a tick on every file.

So two strands from every job never fell on anyone. They were caught during the dwell. That's the only place slack can go before it falls: into a catch, tied by the knotter standing at the site with the fid in his hand. Standards can't see it, because Standards only reads what fell on the keeper. The one thing in the world that shows the gap is a re-swing of the site before the untie.
And the only re-swings are in this drawer, which is his.
I think of Ferdie at fourteen. I think of a pebble untied on Hobday Street every April. Two strands a job, for years, is a great many pebbles.
I photograph six of the pairs, then six more, until my phone complains it's full.
At the very back of the drawer, behind a cardboard divider with no label, there's one more sheet. It isn't a junior's. It's in his hand.
Lantry Steps. Dated four days before my warrant. Two strands. Then, smaller: Half-turn.
He knew. He stood on those steps with his own bob and watched it hesitate, the way mine did, and he wrote it down. Then he sent a clerk who would count two.
Underneath, in pencil, one word and a question mark.
shape?

And beside it, in a different pencil, a small tick and a date. The day I was suspended. The day he walked me down the steps and asked me so kindly how my fall had come, and whether anything odd had happened near me, and I told him everything. The nurse. The defibrillator. The ambulance. My name on the radio.
He wasn't being kind. He was checking his answer.
He sent me to the Lantry Steps so he could watch Orla's snare fire. Not to stop it. To see its shape.
On the stair outside, the football goes quiet. Bev shouts up, "I'm off, love! Half five! Nobody's been on your stair!"
I go to the door. "Thank you, Bev! Really. Thank you so much."
"You're a funny one," she calls, and the yard door bangs, and she's gone.
Then I do what I came for.

The last docket in the sour book has no site. If the site is written anywhere, it's here: a job in Allocation's pending tray with a doorstep or a wall within a mile of Mags. I go through the tray. I go through Vosper's pending folder. I go through the spike on his desk where tomorrow's slips wait. Jobs by the docks. A cracked chimney on Rope Walk. Nothing near the union hall. Nothing near anywhere Mags goes.
It hasn't been filed as a job yet.
That should feel better than it does. A snare doesn't need a file. It needs a knot, a fid and a knotter who knows the pattern. All a file does is give a Porter something to sign.
I close his drawer. I'm sliding my phone into my coat when the main lights come on.
Gervase Vosper is standing in the doorway with his black umbrella furled and dripping, and he doesn't look surprised. He looks pleased, the way you'd look at a guest who's come early to a party.
"Ila," he says. "You found the good cabinet."

I should run. The yard door is at the bottom of the stair. Instead I stand by his desk with my phone in my pocket and my heart in my ears, and there's nobody left to ask to hold anything, because Bev has gone home and I thanked her, and it's just me.
He doesn't call Security. He stands his umbrella in the rack by the door, takes off his gloves one finger at a time, and sits on the corner of a junior's desk as if we have an appointment.

"Four years in Registry," he says, "and you still know where every slip goes. Do you know how rare that is? Most clerks couldn't find their own desks without a docket. Your report on the Lantry Steps was the best thing Registry's sent up this year. I told you so, didn't I?"
"You did." My voice comes out quite ordinary. "Mr Vosper, why did you write 'shape' on your sheet before you sent me?"
He smiles at me warmly, as if I've got something right in an exam.
"I write questions on everything," he says. "It's how I learn. You should try it."
That isn't an answer. We both know it isn't.

"You're suspended," he goes on, gently, "and you're in my office after hours without a pass. If I rang down, Standards would have you out of the building tonight and out of the Bureau by Friday. I'm not going to ring down. I'd much rather do you a favour."
"What favour?"

"Allocation needs someone who reads paper the way you do. A field post. Your own jobs, your own fid. No more filing other people's repairs." He lets that sit between us. "And no exams. Exams are Standards' little ceremony, and Standards owes me a consideration or two."
I want it. I want it so much my chest aches. It's the thing I've wanted every day for four years at a desk in Registry, filing where other people got to go.
And I know the rule, word for word, because for four years I had nothing to do down there but learn it.
"A grade is a licence," I say. "Standards measures your reach at a witnessed practical, and nobody can pass a grade above what was measured. My reach is two. There isn't a field grade for two."
"There's a post for you," says Vosper. "Let me worry about the grade."
"It wouldn't be lawful."
"No," he agrees, quite kindly. "It would be a favour. Favours are how this building works, Ila. You've seen my drawer."
He stands and picks up his gloves.
"The consideration is small. Orla keeps notebooks. She always has. Bring them to me."
I have never said Orla's name in this building. Not once. Not to Stan, not to Standards, and never to him.
He holds the door open for me, the way he did on the front steps, as if I'm the one doing him a favour by leaving.
"Orla Treadgold's notebooks," he says. "All of them. You have till the end of the month."
